It does imply that brains are biological computers, but I think it is completely wrong in that. Searle pretty convincingly showed that computing is something that we find in computers, not something that is performed by them. So it really is a category error, because computers do not compute in any meaningful sense: They are designed to perform operations that we find useful as computations. Completely different thing.

The major question is: Are brains Turing machines. I think it is pretty easy to show that they are not, since there is no easily identifiable tape and the instruction code itself is an output and maleable. This article argues that evolution disqualifies brains as Turing machines, but I am not so sure.

One big issue is that brains seem to be capable of performing hypercomputation, but I am not willing to cede that they are hypercomputers, so I believe that it involves some sort of non-Turing process. Penrose even suggested that quantum gravity may be involved, but that seems fanciful to me. Conversely, I don't think that brains (and certainly not minds) are actually Turing complete unless you allow computers as actual physical extension of minds. Even then...
